title: Level 4 (Expert) - D-6
notes:
West leads the ♥Q against 3NT. West's heart opening lead is won by South. Even if the defenders have to take their ♦A on the first or second round, South will have only 8 tricks (2 hearts, 4 diamonds, and 2 clubs). South will still need an extra club trick (presumably by finessing against the ♣Q) for his 9th trick.

South should lead the ♣A or ♣K at trick 2 (in case West has a singleton ♣Q). When both defenders follow small, South should lead either the ♦Q and overtake with dummy's ♦K, or lead the ♦10 or ♦9 and overtake with dummy's ♦J. When this wins, South should finesse against the ♣Q with East (South needs this finesse in any case). West discards a spade revealing that South must finesse again in order to pick up the clubs.

South leads another diamond and West follows small leaving South with a decision as to which diamond should be played from the dummy. The ♦K will be the winning play if West started with 3 or 4 diamonds to the ♦A. It will win the trick and South can repeat the club finesse to come to 9 tricks.

Playing dummy's ♦K on the second round will be fatal if East was dealt a doubleton ♦A. With the diamond suit blocked South will have no hope of coming to 9 tricks. South could have made his contract on this layout by playing a low diamond from dummy on the second round of the suit. The diamond suit is now unblocked and South will emerge with an overtrick (or 2 overtricks if the defenders fail to cash their 2 spade winners now).

It is correct for South to play dummy's ♦K on the second round of the suit. If diamonds are 3-2, the ♦A is more likely to be with the 3-card holding than with the doubleton. The fact that West could still have 4 diamonds to the ♦A further bolsters the argument in favor of playing dummy's ♦K.
